summary.value: This paper presented the fundamental sources of adversarial vulnerability to be pervasive in the prompt embeddings of concept-erased model inherited from the original model instead of unlearning process. The proposed RECORD coordinate-descent-based restoration algorithm outperforms existing unlearning methods significantly. Extensive experiments shows the compute-performance tradeoff. The analysis of transferability to SDXL and FLUX is a forward-looking plus.

strengths.value:
1. This paper presented the good theoretical analysis of vulnerability for unlearned diffusion models. Adversarial embeddings are pervasive in the prompt space and this vulnerability is from the original model, not created by the unlearning process. The behavior of the text embeddings during embedding-level attack provides good proof of this.
2. Coordinate-descent-based restoration algorithm and two-stage candidate selection (linear approximation + exact evaluation) is a clever and practical solution to the combinatorial problem of a large vocabulary.
3. Extensive experiment setup and ablation study. It benchmarks against a wide array of erasure methods (ESD, FMN, AC, SPM, UCE, AdvUnlearn, RECE, ED, SalUn, SH) and concepts (style, objects, nudity). The 17.8x improvement is a outstanding result.

weaknesses.value:
1. lack of enough quality assessment with for example FID, CLIP score for the unlearned model RECORD result.
2. there is not much describing the adversarial prompt with RECORD will look like. If it's too long and deviate too much from a normal prompt, it will be easily rejected by real image gen system by simple safe guarding before it reaches to the model. Methods that produce semantically coherent adversarial prompts will be desired.
3. RECORD's loss function requires access to the original SD model, which is fine as the a white-box attack assumption but limits the usage or hurt the performance.
4. The claim for converge to a coordinate-wise local minimum requires further discussion. The guarantee is only for the top-k token selection.

questions.value: 1. do you think RECORD can be extended to support other modality instead of text prompt only?

We would like to first thank the reviewer for their insightful reviews and their recognition of the clarity of the paper, the significance of our vulnerability studies, the strong performance of the RECORD algorithm, and the extensiveness of our ablation studies. 

We would like to address the concerns raised by the reviewer below:

> W1: lack of enough quality assessment with for example FID, CLIP score for the unlearned model RECORD result.


Regarding the lack of FID and CLIP score, in this paper we use a very standard approach by assessing the concept restoration quality with a classifier. We would like to politely note that the two metrics are ubiquitously used in concept erasure literature, but rarely in papers on concept restoration methods. We would like to thank the reviewer for their suggestion, and we are happy to present the reviewer with the FID (lower is better) and CLIP (higher is better) scores on Van Gogh experiments. We are willing to extend these experiments upon the further request from the reviewer.

As shown above, RECORD still consistently achieves superior performance over the baseline attack methods. 


> W2: there is not much describing the adversarial prompt with RECORD will look like. If it's too long and deviate too much from a normal prompt, it will be easily rejected by real image gen system by simple safe guarding before it reaches to the model. Methods that produce semantically coherent adversarial prompts will be desired.



We would like to thank the reviewer’s insightful question regarding the fluency of the optimised prompts and the deviation from a normal prompt. We note that this problem remains largely unaddressed by all existing concept restoration methods. Due to the limited time, at time of posting this rebuttal, we are still actively exploring possible methods to improve the fluency of the optimised prompts, and we will update the reviewer once we have further results. 


> W3: RECORD's loss function requires access to the original SD model, which is fine as the a white-box attack assumption but limits the usage or hurt the performance.


We also understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the requirement of access to the original SD model. 
- We would like to note that this requirement can be eliminated by changing the loss function from Equation 4 (requiring the access to the original model) to Equation 3 (uses Gaussian noise instead) in Appendix B. Since Appendix B demonstrates the two loss functions perform very similarly empirically, with Equation 4 outperforming Equation 3 by a small margin in certain scenarios, which demonstrated switching the loss function would not make any significant performance-wise difference, and can be done almost trivially.


- Regarding “limits the usage”, we would also like to politely point out that the white-box assumptions are consistent with that of P4D (uses Equation 4) and very similar to UD (uses Equation 3).  Crucially, in appendix F, we examine the transferability of the successful adversarial prompts on some open-sourced erased models to other completely different black-box models, without requiring the access to the original / concept-erased model weights. We found that RECORD achieves the best performance in **14 out of 18** cases by up to **7 times** (see ESD-VanGogh cell). These results demonstrate the superior transferability and thus black-box capability of RECORD over other baseline algorithms.

comment.value:
> W4: The claim for converge to a coordinate-wise local minimum requires further discussion. The guarantee is only for the top-k token selection.

Thank you for this insightful comment. We agree with the reviewer that evaluating only on the top-k tokens, rather than searching through the entire vocabulary exhaustively may not correspond to a coordinate-wise local minimum. As we only replace tokens when the loss decreases, the loss of our algorithm is strictly monotonically decreasing, but we will rephrase our explanation for clarity upon revision.. Furthermore, the algorithmic design of choosing top-k tokens reflect a tradeoff between the compute and performance, as demonstrated in Table 7 in Appendix D. In the ideal case of infinite compute, where an exhaustive search of the entire  vocabulary can be performed, the algorithm should converge towards a coordinate-wise local minimum. We will clarify this in a future revision. 


> Q1: do you think RECORD can be extended to support other modality instead of text prompt only?


Regarding extending the algorithm to other modalities
- For different input modality: The use of coordinate descent is specifically for handling difficulties in discrete optimization on text tokens. The same issue does not exist in other input modalities such as images, where the pixel values (optimisation space) are naturally continuous and backpropagatable. Adversarial attacks in this case can thus succeed much easier [1].
- For different output modality: we believe the RECORD algorithm is generic enough for extending to other output modalities, e.g. text-to-video, and is a direction we are actively exploring. 

We are delighted to report that we have conducted new additional experiments according to the reviewer’s suggestions. We eagerly await continued feedback, and will follow up with a revised manuscript according to our further discussion with the reviewer. 

We hope the above address the reviewer’s concerns and can help them possibly further adjust their scores. We are happy to discuss if the reviewer has any further concerns. 

[1] Carlini, N., et. al. "Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 36, 61478-61500 (2023).

summary.value: This work proposes a new token-level concept restoration attack (called RECORD) against concept erasure on text-to-image diffusion models. The token-level approach is motivated by the claim that embedding-level attacks are less successful than token-level ones, but this assertion lacks convincing evidence. Token-level, or more specifically, prompt-level attacks are more realistic when assuming only black-box access to jailbreak a potentially erased model; however, RECORD requires white-box access to the gradients. The novel contribution of the RECORD method is a new coordinate-descent approach to reduce the discrete search space for the most potent attack token sequences. When it comes to baselines, this study does not compare to embedding-level attacks, even though it's mentioned that they are less successful than token-level ones, and misses an important erasure method baseline (STEREO, Srivatsan et al. CVPR'25). Despite these limitations, this study primarily appeals with its insightful analysis sections, for example, the one providing evidence for a dense population of adversarial embeddings in the CLIP space, and additional experiments, such as Appendix B, which provide an honest comparison of the two prevailing embedding-level attack approaches. Overall, this study provides value to the community; however, the primary focus, which is the RECORD algorithm, requires more clarity on its motivation (token-level vs. embedding-level), additional experiments (including more baselines and targets), and a more thorough and fair comparison to related methods.

strengths.value:
- (S1) **Insightful Analyses** in Section 3.2 and in most sections of the Appendix, especially in A, B and G.
- (S2) **Creative Visualisations** that help to illustrate the main arguments made in the paper, especially Figures 1, 2 and 4.
- (S3) **Experiments beyond SD v1.4** on the transferability to newer architectures of attack prompts derived from SD v1.4. or even qualitative results of applying RECORD directly to FLUX or SDXL.

weaknesses.value:
I find the following list of things to be major weaknesses:
- (W1) **Unclear claims** of superiority of (white-box) token-level attacks over embedding-level attacks (in lines 295-296). What does superior performance mean here? As far as I am informed, embedding-level attacks, such as CCE, are more effective than token-level ones.
- (W2) **Justification for white-box token-level attack**: RECORD requires access to model gradients and is therefore a white-box method. Attacks often employ a token/prompt-level approach because they do not want to assume white-box access to the model or the system. This is why I was wondering how a token-level attack, such as RECORD, realistically justifies its white-box assumption. The transferability of optimized token sequences (prompts) to different models could potentially be used to justify the white-box setting of token-level approaches, as somewhat demonstrated in Table 10; however, the superiority of RECORD over existing attacks is questionable here.
- (W3) **Missing baselines**: CCE as an inversion-based attack baseline and STEREO as an inversion-robust erasure baseline.
- (W4) **Unclear fairness of comparison to baselines**: The comparison is either not fair or not clear enough w.r.t. to the compute-effectiveness trade-off
	- RECORD with J=64 requires a lot more runtime than P4D and UD (see Table 8 in the Appendix).
	- How well would RECORD perform when J is chosen such that the runtime / compute requirements are on par with P4D or UD? Is there a difference, and if yes, is it significantly better?

The following are minor weaknesses:
- (W5) **SH is missing in some tables**: For example, SH is not shown for the "van gogh" scenario in Table 3 (top). Is RECORD failing against it?
- (W6) **Limited evaluation scope** w.r.t. to the targets that are considered (only Van Gogh for style, only three object classes); no explicit content erasure or celebrity erasure scenarios.
- (W7) **Scattered results**: This paper could benefit hugely from compiling the results into an easier-to-grasp and coherent picture by avoiding the numerous scattered tables with often inconsistent baselines throughout the tables/figures.
- (W8) **Only anecdotal results on FLUX/SDXL** to demonstrate the applicability of RECORD on these architectures.

questions.value: - (Q1) Rename "Embed Attack 1" (black-box?) and "Embed Attack 2" (white-box?) to something more meaningful and add citations to most prominent works that use them to the tables.

We would like to thank the reviewer for carefully reading our manuscript and providing valuable feedback, their appreciation of the insightful analysis into the model vulnerability, and the recognition of the values of the paper to the community. We hope our responses to be helpful in addressing the reviewer's concerns. 

First, We would like to respectfully and carefully clarify a potential misunderstanding in the review. The reviewer states 
> “...embedding-level attacks are less successful than token-level ones, but this assertion lacks convincing evidence”
> ”this study does not compare to embedding-level attacks, even though it's mentioned that they are less successful than token-level ones” 

We respectfully disagree with this. First, we do have results for embedding-level attacks in Table 4 of Appendix B . More importantly, we never assert they ‘are less successful than token-level ones’ in the paper, it also contradicts the reviewer’s later statement that 

> “Appendix B, which provide an honest comparison of the two prevailing embedding-level attack approaches”

For the below, we want to clarify the following points (related to the reviewer’s concerns): (1) the comparison between embedding-level and token-level attacks; (2) the realisticity of the embedding- / token-level attacks.

Appendix B (mainly for comparing different loss functions) demonstrates that embedding-level attacks can easily achieve better ASR (and thus performance-wise more successful). However, this is because embedding-level attacks address a very different problem from the prompt-level ones, in that the optimization space is continuous and differentiable. This echoes with the prior works that demonstrate it is far easier to optimize in the continuous space (image) than in the discrete space (text) when adversarially attacking multimodal LLMs [1].

However, as stated in **line 194 - 195**, precise inversions from embeddings to prompts are not guaranteed to exist, and we thus argue that embedding-level attacks perform better (as per Appendix B), but less realistic. 

> “prompt-level attacks are more realistic when assuming only black-box access”. 

We fully respect the reviewer’s opinion, but we only partially agree with this statement. Although a tech-savvy adversary may be able to condition the model on embedding level for a white-box model, typical adversarial users may only use text prompting to attack models. We thus argue that prompt-level attacks are still highly relevant even in the white-box setting. In addition, our paper includes studies on black-box transferability of RECORD, as acknowledged by the reviewer. Such transferability is not possible for embedding-level attacks with different tokenizers or text encoders between two models, or to black box scenarios where only text prompts are accepted. Therefore in our work, we made apple-to-apple comparisons between prompt-level attacks, such as P4D, UD and RECORD. 

We will now address the numbered weaknesses below.


> W1: **Unclear claims** of superiority of (white-box) token-level attacks over embedding-level attacks (in lines 295-296). What does superior performance mean here? As far as I am informed, embedding-level attacks, such as CCE, are more effective than token-level ones.

We sincerely apologise for any confusion, and we are happy to rephrase our claims. We will attempt to clarify them below. Line 295 - 296 makes the claim that coordinate-descent-based attacks (e.g. ARCA) perform better than projection-based attacks (e.g. GBDA). We cite papers to back up this claim e.g. [1, 2]. Importantly, both approaches find adversarial prompts (not embeddings), and we thus consider both are of prompt-level attacks. We thus do not make the claim that “superiority of (white-box) token-level attacks over embedding-level attacks (in lines 295-296)” 
We would like to kindly note that all works cited between **line 294 - 297** assumes white-box access to the model, and we will address CCE-related concerns in **W3**.

> W3: Missing baselines: CCE as an inversion-based attack baseline and STEREO as an inversion-robust erasure baseline.

We appreciate the reviewer for the constructive comment. RECORD is a prompt-level attack, which searches for adversarial prompts via discrete optimisation in the text space, which is far more difficult. CCE, on the other hand, is an embedding-level attack, which finds adversarial embeddings in the continuous space, which is far easier, does not guarantee the exact invertibility from the embeddings to tokens, and thus poses a different problem from the prompt-level attacks. Therefore, it will not be an apple-to-apple comparison between RECORD and CCE. However, the experiments we have in **Appendix B** (where we cite CCE in **line 750**)  are essentially the same as CCE’s setting without the negative prompts, which is to find the adversarial embeddings of the erased methods.. Appendix B also compares with other loss functions to explore which loss function performs better under the embedding-level attack setting, which extends beyond the original CCE’s setting.

We refer this to a table made by the previous work [3] (https://github.com/OPTML-Group/AdvUnlearn): methods such as ED, SalUN, SH, are for erasing object-related concepts, rather than style-related ones. We are happy to add some more  concepts upon the reviewer’s further request, although we already include an explicit concept (nudity). summary.value:
This paper reassesses the robustness of concept-erased diffusion models and argues that existing concept erasure techniques are fundamentally vulnerable—not because the erasure is ineffective, but because adversarial prompt embeddings capable of restoring erased concepts are widely scattered in the embedding space and largely inherited from the original pretrained model. This reframes the problem: concept erasure does not eliminate latent pathways for restoration, and current evaluations may underestimate attacker capability.

To substantiate this argument, the authors propose RECORD, a white-box, token-level concept restoration attack that replaces the standard projection-based gradient optimization with a tangential coordinate descent strategy. By selecting tokens directly in discrete space through a two-stage ranking-and-evaluation procedure, RECORD avoids projection errors and search-space mismatch that hamper prior methods like P4D and UnlearnDiffAtk.

strengths.value:
1. The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and easy to follow, making both the motivation and technical contributions accessible to the reader.
2. The work provides an insightful reframing of the vulnerability in concept erasure, highlighting that restoration pathways are largely inherited from pretrained models rather than being caused by the erasure methods themselves.
3. The proposed discrete token-level coordinate descent attack is well-motivated and achieves strong performance, outperforming prior methods and establishing new state-of-the-art results.

weaknesses.value:
1. The evaluation includes a limited number of erased concepts compared to the experimental settings used in prior baselines. Expanding the set of concepts would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.
2. It would be valuable to include comparisons with more text-encoder-based defense methods. While AdvUnlearn is included, methods such as SAFREE and others are omitted, and adding these would provide a more comprehensive assessment of defense robustness.

questions.value: 1. Can the proposed method be extended to the text-to-video (T2V) setting? Since the attack operates on the text embedding space, it seems feasible that the approach could transfer to T2V models as well. The authors’ thoughts on this potential extension would be appreciated.

Unfortunately, we note that the SAFREE paper does not provide the code for running the attacks, nor sufficient details regarding the attacks in their paper for replication. Below we will try to clarify the potential differences in the evaluation protocol with some speculation on the SAFREE’s experimental setting

There are a few reasons which may have caused discrepancies, the main one is due to the different experiment setup: 


1. We observe that e.g. for UnlearnDiffAtk (UD) on ESD, SAFREE paper reports 76.1% in Table 1. This aligns with the number reported in UD's original paper (76.05%). However, UD’s evaluation process may differ quite significantly from ours. UD’s code generates one image to evaluate the prompt every one of its 50 optimization steps, and stops immediately when one image is deemed nude by e.g. a NudeNet classifier. This means each prompt gets evaluated 50 times throughout the optimisation, which generally boosts the ASR. From our experience, it also leads to a significant number of false positives. We note that, if the prompt is only evaluated once at the end of the 50 steps, the ASR can decrease by 3 times (in the case of ESD, to 26.2% vs 76.1% in SAFREE’s paper). A similar technique is also used in P4D’s original codebase, where each prompt generates 3 images, and is deemed unsafe if one of the three images contains the erased unsafe concept. In our experiments, we only evaluate each optimised prompt at the end of the optimisation once by generating 10 images, and reporting the percentage of the unsafe images over the total number of images generated, as stated in **line 419**. This should be the main reason where the discrepancy comes from. 

2. The followings  are relatively minor differences between the implementations: For any concept erasure methods requiring finetuning, model weights may differ; We use a different set of target prompts from I2P; Because we do not use I2P, we also do not fix the seed when running the experiments; We use a diffusion classifier rather than NudeNet for evaluating the ASR. 

Furthermore, to address any concerns related to the differences between the evaluation processes, we have included **Table 9 in Appendix F** in our initial submission where we tried to evaluate RECORD against P4D and UD under UD’s evaluation pipeline (where each prompt is evaluated 50 times in total) with I2P prompts and NudeNet. We found that under this approach, RECORD can still demonstrate superior performance over other baseline attack methods.  

We hope our response classifies any concern from the reviewer. We are happy to discuss further if the reviewer has other questions.

comment.value:
We would like to first thank the reviewer for their appreciation of the clarity of the paper, our vulnerability study, as well as the importance of the vulnerability of the concept erasure topic. 

We would like to address the concerns raised by the reviewer below:

> W1: The method is somewhat easy. The experiments in Sec 3.1 and 3.2 are intuitive and persuasive, although previous studies have shown this point. However, the proposed method is only borrowed from recent studies, just as the cited papers in Line 296. The authors did not introduce any novel method based on their empirical observation. 

Regarding the methodology, we acknowledge RECORD is inspired by optimization techniques on adversarial attacks of language models in **line 151**, but there is no guarantee that similar methods would work for concept restoration in text-to-image diffusion models prior to our work. We also acknowledge that coordinate descent is a classic optimization technique. We would like to politely note that our work is the first that applies the coordinate descent algorithm in the field of concept restoration, and observed significant improvement over the baselines through extensive experimentation and ablation studies. Significant work is involved for transferring such ideas to the modality of text-to-image generation, and we rigorously justified the algorithmic design in Appendix B, C, D, and demonstrated the superior performance of RECORD. 


Rather than exploring sophisticated new strategies for concept restoration, this paper demonstrates the effectiveness of using classical and simple optimization (i.e. coordinate descent) to address new and challenging questions (i.e. does direct token optimization outperform projection based methods on image generators? Are the results generalizable? Are adversarial prompts transferable to black-box models?).

Furthermore, our work also investigates the root cause of vulnerability in concept-erased models, the first of its kind and a novel contribution of our paper as well. We consider the significant gain of performance over previous SOTA achieved with classic and intuitive optimisation techniques to be a strength of this work.

comment.value:
> W2: The evaluation is unfair and insufficient to some extent. The used metric is based on the denoising errors. However, the proposed attacking method is also based on the denoising errors. This has resulted in an optimization process in the evaluation method. Also, the results in Tab 2 reveal that this metric is not accuracy. For nudity, it only achieves 87.6% accuracy. Why not to use the common concept detectors such as NudeNet? It is trained on large data and therefore has excellent detection ability.

Regarding the review’s concern on the classifier used in the evaluation process, we motivate the use of diffusion classifiers in **line 349 - 353**, that we attempt to propose a single, unified evaluation model over a large ensemble of different classifiers from different sources for different concepts, potentially introducing inconsistencies. 

Regarding “The used metric is based on the denoising errors. However, the proposed attacking method is also based on the denoising errors”, we respectfully disagree that this leads to any unfair comparison. 

First, we would like to politely point out that the loss functions of all restoration methods (P4D, UD, RECORD) are based on denoising errors. In fact, UD’s loss function (Equation 3 in Appendix B) is more similar to the objective of the diffusion classifier (stated in Section 4.1) than that of RECORD or P4D (Equation 4 in Appendix B). We totally understand where the reviewer’s concern is coming from, and if what the reviewer said were true, then our current setup is unfairly advantaging UD over P4D or RECORD. However, as we will demonstrate below, this concern is not true.

Secondly, our ablation study in Appendix B demonstrates UD’s loss function (Equation 3) marginally underperforms when compared with P4D’s / RECORD’s (Equation 4). We therefore evidently believe that this experiment eliminates concerns regarding any unfair evaluation due to the similarity between the objectives of the attacking and the evaluation method, and that the evaluation process does not unfairly advantage or disadvantage any methods in any of our experiments.

Thirdly, regarding the accuracy of the diffusion classifier, we rigorously examined its robustness during the early stage of the project. For NudeNet with a configuration in line with those used in P4D and UD repositories, it achieves an accuracy of **89.8%**, which is very similar to the **87.6%** of the diffusion classifier we used. We would like to further re-assure the reviewer that if there had been any problem regarding the use of the diffusion classifier, we would have (almost trivially) switched back to the traditional classifiers e.g. NudeNet. Instead, we hope this can be counted as one of the contributions of our work.

We are happy to discuss this if the reviewer has any further concerns.

> Question: Considering that the authors explored the behaviors of the text embeddings, can we optimize a loss function only on text encoders?

We sincerely thank the reviewer for carefully reading our paper and providing a very interesting question regarding the feasibility of optimising only on the text encoders, firstly, strategies like “optimising a loss function only on text encoders” are only possible if the erasure method modifies the text encoder (the mapping of the texts to embedding is changed), but not possible if only the denoiser is modified (the mapping remains unchanged). This narrows the question to a simpler objective of searching for the same original text embedding with a concept-erased text encoder, i.e. $\min_{y’} \|\mathcal T(y) - \mathcal T’(y’) \|$, where $\mathcal T$ and $\mathcal T’$ corresponds to the original / concept-erased text encoder, $y$ corresponds to the original erased concept.  We would expect this to underperform, as the optimisation neglects the essential signal from the denoiser on “how the final image might look”, and will only try to find one single embedding $\mathcal T(y)$, which can be very difficult, rather than exploiting other embeddings far-away from $\mathcal T(y)$ that can generate the same erased concept as explained in section 3.2. Indeed our embedding-level attack as shown in the table below confirms this hypothesis, and the difference in performance is rather significant.

| **Denoiser + Text Encoder** (Ours, Table 4 in paper) | **99.0** | **100.0** | **92.6** | **44.8** | **96.8** |

Unfortunately we are unable to engage with you due to the sudden ICLR rule change. We would like to summarise below 

- We believe our clarifications have addressed your concerns regarding the novelty of RECORD, the first coordinate-descent algorithm for concept restoration. We are also confident that our vulnerability study, which demonstrates its **pervasiveness** and the further insights into its **origin** is the first of its kind in this field. 
- We have also provided new results regarding NudeNet, which demonstrates the competitive performance of our diffusion classifier, and continues to demonstrate the significantly superior performance of RECORD. We thank you for acknowledging that your initial concerns regarding evaluation fairness has been addressed. 
- We have provided additional experiments testing the text-encoder-loss-only approach, which did not work. We thank you for acknowledging that this question has also been addressed. 

We hope our clarification, together with the new results, can address all of your concerns and further convince you about the contribution of our paper. 

Sincerely,

Authors of 13764

display_title: Meta Review of Submission13764 by Area Chair AXt5

summary.value: The reviewers’ concerns mainly focus on limited methodological novelty and technical insight. The proposed approach builds on existing embedding perturbation and adversarial optimization techniques without introducing a fundamentally new method. Reviewers also note that the experimental scope is narrower than in some prior work, raising questions about generality. Reviewers remain unconvinced that the analysis establishes the root cause of vulnerabilities in concept-erased models.

reviewer_concerns.value: The core optimization strategy is adapted from existing embedding perturbation and adversarial prompt optimization techniques. In addition, although the paper provides extensive empirical evidence on the pervasiveness and inheritance of vulnerabilities in concept-erased models, the claim of identifying the root cause of these vulnerabilities remains partially unresolved. The current analysis characterizes the phenomenon rather than offering a definitive causal or theoretical explanation.

reviewer_scores.value: The additional experiments and clarifications would partially address concerns about evaluation fairness and empirical validity, but the central issues regarding methodological novelty, technical insight, and claims about root causes would remain. Reviewers might have adjusted their scores slightly upward, but most likely only to the level of a borderline reject, rather than to a clear accept.
